rationale: Original abstract describes ginger for dopamine-agonist nausea and dyskinesia in drug context. Open bibliography gives a ginger nausea review. Publisher nominal PDF is a subscription preview, so the original body and inline context remain open.

Review discusses gait velocity in cerebral small vessel disease at line 139 and Parkinson as a disease risk context at line 97, but does not discuss black tea or any tea exposure, nor a tea-versus-walking outcome.
MPTP mouse study injects corn oil as vehicle for magnolol and in sham and lesion groups. Striatal VMAT2 PET is measured; no isolated oral oil or clinical bradykinesia contrast.
Narrative review names corn oil as possible source of lipid oxidation products; no clinical corn oil bradykinesia comparison.
Genetically modified mouse study injects tamoxifen dissolved in corn oil for gene inactivation and measures synaptic changes, not oral oil or Parkinson bradykinesia.
Rotenone Parkinson model injects rotenone in DMSO and corn oil; nicotine groups and motor outcomes are compared, without an isolated oral corn oil effect.
Curcumin review lists corn oil as vehicle in multiple rodent Parkinson models, often for rotenone or treatment, with locomotor assays; no direct refined oral corn oil human bradykinesia estimate.
Natural-product Parkinson review names thyme as a source of general terpenoids; passiflora catalepsy is a different plant and no dried thyme anxiety study is reported.
Zebrafish flavonoid review identifies thyme as a luteolin source; animal flavonoid tests are not an oral dried thyme anxiety intervention.

Original 2025 T. ciliatus essential oil injected into BPA-treated rats reports open-field and light-dark behavior; species, concentrated oil, injection, model and uncertain light-dark interpretation limit transfer to dried culinary thyme and Parkinson anxiety.
Flavonoid neurodegeneration review lists thyme as a source of luteolin; no dried thyme clinical anxiety comparison.
Ethnobotany review describes traditional T. vulgaris for digestive and respiratory ailments, not a measured anxiety treatment.
Polyphenol review cites thyme as a chemical source; no oral dried thyme or anxiety comparison.

Full archived review body inspected. It mentions olive oil only as an agricultural rotenone-residue finding (citing Cabras et al. 2002) and mentions stride length in separate pesticide-model discussion; it does not test olive-oil exposure, Parkinson gait, or an olive-related motor endpoint. Lexical collision; no cold-pressed oil or matched outcome.

Full archived review body inspected. This is a wearable-sensor technology bibliometric/narrative review. Olive oil appears as a food-grade biosensor matrix for GI glucose monitoring; gait is reviewed as another sensor application. No dietary exposure, Parkinson cohort, or stride outcome linked to olive oil.

Full archived review body inspected. It reviews capillary-electrophoresis methods for fatty-acid analysis; flaxseed/linseed oil is an analytic sample/material, while constipation occurs in unrelated introductory discussion of short-chain fatty acids. No oral flaxseed-oil intervention or measured constipation outcome.

Full archived Parkinson gut-microbiome review inspected. It describes constipation as a common PD symptom and cites a separate trial of 1,000 mg flaxseed-derived omega-3 plus 400 IU vitamin E; that combination trial reports total UPDRS and biomarkers, not constipation severity and not pure oil. Related PD/formulation context only.

Full archived PD ferroptosis review inspected. It notes constipation as a prodromal PD symptom and summarizes the same flaxseed-derived omega-3 + vitamin E trial with broad UPDRS/metabolic results. It does not report a bowel outcome or isolate oil. Its table points to NCT04491383, but that official ID is an unrelated tocotrienol trial; do not use it as registration evidence for the 2017 flaxseed study.

The whole-diet protocol recommends extra-virgin olive oil. Its Supplementary Table S1 and official registry verify scheduled GSRS constipation symptoms and separate Bristol stool form. Trial results and individual oil intake remain pending.

The original plans sensor-based same-foot stride length and height-normalized stride in a diet/activity factorial comparison. Supplemental visits verify when measured. Oil grade beyond extra-virgin and actual participant intake remain unverified. No results posted.

The protocol specifies sensor walking speed and the official registry separately lists a ten-meter walking test. The visit supplement confirms both measurements, with whole-diet olive oil guidance and no results posted.
